If there were 15 bike trips from Station A at 8:00 AM, there will probably be \~15 trips at 9:00 AM. We can use this temporal persistence to improve predictions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sort by station and time study_panel <- study_panel %>% arrange(start_station, interval60) # Create lag variables WITHIN each station study_panel <- study_panel %>% group_by(start_station) %>% mutate( lag1Hour = lag(Trip_Count, 1), lag2Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 2), lag3Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 3), lag12Hours = lag(Trip_Count, 12), lag1day = lag(Trip_Count, 24) ) %>% ungroup() # Remove rows with NA lags (first 24 hours for each station) study_panel_complete <- study_panel %>% filter(!is.na(lag1day)) cat("Rows after removing NA lags:", format(nrow(study_panel_complete), big.mark = ","), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows after removing NA lags: 605,298 ``` ::: ::: ### Visualize Lag Correlations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sample one station to visualize # Sample one station to visualize example_station <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(start_station == first(start_station)) %>% head(168) # One week # Plot actual vs lagged demand ggplot(example_station, aes(x = interval60)) + geom_line(aes(y = Trip_Count, color = "Current"), linewidth = 1) + geom_line(aes(y = lag1Hour, color = "1 Hour Ago"), linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.7) + geom_line(aes(y = lag1day, color = "24 Hours Ago"), linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.7) + scale_color_manual(values = c( "Current" = "#08519c", "1 Hour Ago" = "#3182bd", "24 Hours Ago" = "#6baed6" )) + labs( title = "Temporal Lag Patterns at One Station", subtitle = "Past demand predicts future demand", x = "Date-Time", y = "Trip Count", color = "Time Period" ) + plotTheme ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Chen_Xiaoqing_Assignment5_files/figure-html/lag_correlations-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Temporal Train/Test Split **CRITICAL:** We must train on PAST data and test on FUTURE data! ### Why Temporal Validation Matters In real operations, at 6:00 AM on March 15, we need to predict demand for March 15-31. We have data from Jan 1 - March 14, but NOT from March 15-31 (it hasn't happened yet!). **Wrong approach:** Train on weeks 10-13, test on weeks 1-9 (predicting past from future!) **Correct approach:** Train on weeks 1-9, test on weeks 10-13 (predicting future from past) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Split by week # Q4 has weeks 40-53 (Oct-Dec) # Train on weeks 40-49 (Jan 1 - early Dec) # Test on weeks 50-53 (rest of Dec) # Which stations have trips in BOTH early and late periods? early_stations <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week < 50) %>% filter(Trip_Count > 0) %>% distinct(start_station) %>% pull(start_station) late_stations <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week >= 50) %>% filter(Trip_Count > 0) %>% distinct(start_station) %>% pull(start_station) # Keep only stations that appear in BOTH periods common_stations <- intersect(early_stations, late_stations) # Filter panel to only common stations study_panel_complete <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(start_station %in% common_stations) # NOW create train/test split train <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week < 50) test <- study_panel_complete %>% filter(week >= 50) cat("Training observations:", format(nrow(train), big.mark = ","), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Training observations: 410,628 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Testing observations:", format(nrow(test), big.mark = ","), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Testing observations: 171,684 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Training date range:", min(train$date), "to", max(train$date), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Training date range: 19997 to 20065 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Testing date range:", min(test$date), "to", max(test$date), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Testing date range: 20066 to 20088 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Adding demographics, station fixed effects, and rush-hour interactions (Models 3–5) did not meaningfully improve test-set accuracy, which suggests that most of the predictable structure in Q4 2024 demand is already captured by simple temporal patterns, weather, and short-term history. In Part 3, I extended this baseline with three features motivated by the error analysis: a holiday indicator (`is_holiday`), a weekend–good-weather interaction (`weekend_good_weather`), and distance to Center City (`dist_center_km`). The extended model (Model 6) achieved a test-set MAE of about 0.416, slightly worse than the 0.401 MAE of Model 2, so the new features did not improve out-of-sample performance. ## Why Model 6 did not improve MAE Several factors may explain why Model 6 underperforms Model 2. The new variables are partly redundant with existing ones: holiday and weekend–weather effects overlap with weekend and lag terms, and distance to Center City correlates with demographic patterns considered earlier. Adding highly correlated predictors can increase variance and fit noise without adding much new information. In addition, major holidays and “perfect” weekend weather hours make up only a small share of Q4 data, so the model may be overfitting a few unusual days rather than learning general patterns. This comparison highlights an important lesson: statistically significant coefficients in the training data do not guarantee better predictions. Feature engineering should ultimately be evaluated using test-set metrics such as MAE, not just in-sample fit. ## Future directions If I were to extend this work, I would try models that better handle count data and non-linear relationships, such as Poisson or negative-binomial regression and tree-based methods (random forests or gradient boosting). These could capture sharp drops on very cold or rainy days and complex interactions more flexibly than a linear model. I would also consider using a longer time span (multiple quarters or a full year) and richer spatial context, such as bike-lane density or land-use patterns, as well as rolling history features (e.g., 7-day moving averages). Any added complexity, however, should be justified by clear improvements in out-of-sample accuracy.
